Chambishi Copper Smelter Ltd Announces Major Expansion, Boosting Zambia’s Mining Sector

Chambishi Copper Smelter Ltd has unveiled plans for a major expansion at its copper processing facility in Zambia’s Copperbelt Province, signalling a vote of confidence in the country’s mining sector and bringing hopes of new jobs and increased export revenues.

The company announced on Thursday that it will invest $180 million over the next two years to increase its smelting capacity by 40 percent, allowing it to process up to 500,000 tonnes of copper concentrate annually once the project is completed in late 2026. The expansion will include the installation of state-of-the-art smelting technology, new environmental management systems, and the construction of additional storage and logistics infrastructure at the Chambishi site.

“At Chambishi Copper Smelter Ltd, we are committed to supporting Zambia’s ambitions to become a regional leader in copper production and value addition,” said general manager Joseph Chanda at a press briefing in Kitwe. “This expansion demonstrates our long-term commitment to the Copperbelt and to Zambia as a whole. It will create over 400 direct construction jobs and an estimated 120 permanent positions once operational.”

The announcement has been welcomed by local authorities and industry observers, who see the move as a sign of renewed investor confidence in the country’s mining sector following recent government efforts to streamline regulations and improve fiscal stability.

“We are delighted to see such significant investment in our province,” said Copperbelt Province Minister Lackson Kasonde. “This expansion will not only create much-needed jobs for our youth but also generate additional revenue for local suppliers and contractors.”

Industry analysts note that the expansion comes at a time when global copper demand is expected to rise, driven by the growth of electric vehicles and renewable energy projects worldwide. According to the Zambia Chamber of Mines, the country’s copper output reached 830,000 tonnes in 2023, making it Africa’s second-largest producer after the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“This type of investment is crucial if Zambia is to maintain its competitiveness on the global stage,” said mining analyst Ruth Mulenga. “Modernising facilities and increasing local processing capacity will help Zambia capture more value from its mineral resources.”

Local trade unions have also expressed support for the project, emphasizing the importance of fair labour practices and skills development. “We look forward to working closely with management to ensure that new jobs created offer decent wages and opportunities for training,” said Francis Banda, secretary of the Copperbelt Mineworkers’ Union.

Construction on the expansion is set to begin in August, with the first phase expected to come online by mid-2025.
